newsitem.title: GERMANY: After the party, D.Telekom must get down to work.
newsitem.headline: After the party, D.Telekom must get down to work.

text.p: Now that the party is over for Deutsche Telekom AG, which debuted on stock exchanges in Frankfurt, Tokyo and New York this week in the world's second-largest stock flotation, it will have to give investors good reason to stay on board.

After shares in the telecommunications giant surged 19 percent to close at 33.90 marks on its first day of trade on Monday, Frankfurt traders began taking hefty profits in busy trade on Tuesday, shaving more than five percent off Telekom's share price by midday.
Telekom's shares slipped 5.4 percent in floor trade to close at 32.07 marks, well above the 28.50 mark issue price.

While that sell-off was no surprise, analysts said the jury was still out on Telekom as a long-term investment and on whether the company would cut debt and raise revenues despite heightened competition, to provide healthy returns.
"They are going to have to live up to their forecasts for revenue growth and reduce their debt as they've promised," said Jonathan Shantry, European telecoms analyst at Credit Lyonnais.
A Frankfurt analyst, who asked not to be identified, echoed those comments, saying: "Now they've got to do all the things they promised."
Deutsche Telekom, Europe's largest telecommunications group, made a $13 billion stock issue this week, putting 26 percent of its capital in public hands for the first time.

The issue, the largest-ever in Europe and second in the world only to Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, whipped up enormous popular support, with around two million ordinary Germans buying just under half of the offering.

This squeezed institutional investors. Unable to get as many shares from the offer as they wanted, funds whose holdings are linked to the DAX index of 30 blue-chips were forced to buy Telekom shares on the market to keep their portfolios balanced.
But next year other European telecommunications flotations are scheduled that will give investors a broader choice.

France Telecom, France's most profitable company, plans to float 25 percent of its capital in April. And Italy's Societa Finanziaria Telefonica PA (STET), is expected to complete its privatisation by the end of the year.
One of the main concerns of investors ahead of the listing was Deutsche Telekom's mountain of debt. One of the world's largest debtors, it owes a net $67.64 billion.
By comparison, its main European rival, British Telecom has debt of $3.32 billion and Telekom's strategic partner France Telecom has debt of $16.63 billion.
Analysts said the proceeds from the share listing, if applied to reduce debt, would be a good start towards bringing the company back into line with its European rivals.
The company says its large cash flow and expected profits from previous loss-makers such as the east German phone network and cable television will allow it to easily pay back debts.
While still sceptical, analysts say Telekom is moving in the right direction.

"It's not going to be easy, but their cash flow is reasonable. One significant variable is how much money they'll spend on investments outside of Germany," said Standard and Poor's telecoms analyst Rupert Atkinson.
Indeed, in order to offset competition at home, Telekom is making huge investments abroad. It wants to generate 20 percent of its revenues outside of Germany in the medium term.
Deutsche Telekom knows it has its work cut out for it.

As its shares began trading, Telekom's chief executive Ron Sommer was already thinking about the future, promising investors that dividend yields will be commensurate with profits and vowing to slash debt by a third in four years.

"We will exercise caution and foresight with the capital that has been placed at our disposal. And we will concentrate all of our efforts to further increase the value of our company in the interests of our shareholders," he said.
